shortDescription: Two councils of bishops, first at Carthage and then at Rome, decided how Christians who had given way in the persecution under the emperor Decius could come back to the church: through long penance, with each case examined. The council at Rome also cut off Novatian, a rival bishop of Rome, and his followers.

timeline.headline: Decius's order, and the many who gave way
timeline.witness: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, writing from hiding and soon after

lines.text: Under the emperor Decius, at the first threats, a very great number of Christians at Carthage give up their faith. Many run to the forum to sacrifice of their own accord, and some beg the officials not to put them off as evening comes.
lines.reference: Cyprian, On the Lapsed 7 to 8; Socrates of Constantinople, Church History IV.28, for the persecution Decius raised

lines.text: Some offer the sacrifice. Others pay an official for a certificate saying they had, so as not to sacrifice.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus (Letter 55 in Hartel's Latin) 14

lines.text: Confessors, Christians jailed or tortured for the faith, are pressed to hand out written pardons; Cyprian says thousands are given each day, with no one's case examined.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to the clergy at Rome (Letter 20 in Hartel's Latin) 2

lines.text: The confessors write to Cyprian that they have granted peace to all whose conduct since their fall satisfies him, and ask him to make it known to the other bishops.
lines.reference: Letter of the confessors to Cyprian (Letter 23 in Hartel's Latin)

lines.text: Cyprian puts off any decision on the lapsed until the bishops can meet, and warns that anyone who gives them communion before the council will himself be kept from communion.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 4

lines.text: The clergy at Rome, in a letter Novatian wrote, add that peace should be given to the lapsed who are sick and at the point of death.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 5

timeline.headline: A lax party at Carthage, and two bishops at Rome

lines.text: At Carthage the deacon Felicissimus and five presbyters invite the lapsed to a false peace, telling them to leave off their prayers and pleading. Cyprian calls it another persecution, and holds to the agreement that nothing new be done until all meet and fix a sentence tempered with discipline and mercy.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to the people of Carthage (Letter 43 in Hartel's Latin) 2 to 3

lines.text: At Rome, Cornelius is made bishop by sixteen bishops, and a stricter party sets up Novatian against him.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 24; Socrates of Constantinople, Church History IV.28

lines.text: Novatian writes to all the churches that those who sacrificed must not be admitted to the sacred mysteries, but urged to repent, their pardon left to God.
lines.reference: Socrates of Constantinople, Church History IV.28
lines.note: Socrates, writing almost two centuries later and kind to Novatian's church, reports it from Novatian's letters.

lines.text: Novatian's envoys reach Carthage. Cyprian and the bishops gathered with him keep them from communion.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Cornelius (Letter 44 in Hartel's Latin; Letter 40 in the English) 1

timeline.headline: The council at Carthage chooses a middle way
timeline.witness: Cyprian, who called the council and defended it, in his Letter to Antonianus and later letters

lines.text: A large number of African bishops meet at Carthage. With the Scriptures brought forward on both sides, they choose a middle way: hope of peace is not denied to the lapsed, penance is long, and each case is examined.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 6

lines.text: Those who took certificates are admitted in the meantime, after their case is examined; those who sacrificed are given peace at the point of death.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 17

lines.text: Those who had not repented, and ask for peace only when sickness and danger come, are refused.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 23

lines.text: The heads of the decisions are written in a little book, which Cyprian sends on.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 6

lines.text: Felicissimus and the five presbyters are cut off by the judgment of the bishops.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Cornelius on Fortunatus and Felicissimus (Letter 59 in Hartel's Latin) 9

lines.text: The bishops write to Cornelius at Rome, so that the number of African bishops will not seem too few.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 6

timeline.headline: The council at Rome agrees, and cuts off Novatian's party
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, summing up Cornelius's letters

lines.text: Sixty bishops meet at Rome, with a great many more presbyters and deacons, while bishops of the other provinces give their views where they are.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.43.2

lines.text: The council declares Novatian and his followers strangers to the church, and tells the churches to heal the fallen with the medicines of repentance.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.43.2

lines.text: Cornelius, holding a council with very many bishops, agrees with the African bishops' decision.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 6

timeline.headline: A charge against Cyprian, rival bishops at Carthage, and peace for all who kept repenting

lines.text: Antonianus, a bishop in Africa, is shaken by Novatian's letters. Cyprian writes to clear himself of the thought that he had turned from his early severity to make peace easy for the fallen.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus 1 to 3

lines.text: At Alexandria, Dionysius orders that the dying who ask for remission should receive it, and tells of the old man Serapion, who had sacrificed and was given the eucharist as he died.
lines.reference: Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Church History VI.44

lines.text: At Carthage, the lax party has the presbyter Fortunatus, one of the five, as its bishop, and Novatian's party makes the presbyter Maximus its bishop.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Cornelius on Fortunatus and Felicissimus 9
lines.note: Cyprian's account; he calls Fortunatus a false bishop set up by a few.

lines.text: With a new persecution drawing near, the African bishops write to Cornelius that they will now give peace to all who never left the church and kept repenting from the first day of their fall, so that they are armed for the battle.
lines.reference: Cyprian and the African bishops, synodal letter to Cornelius (Letter 57 in Hartel's Latin) 1 to 3
lines.note: The letter gives no year. Hefele, a modern historian of the councils, dates it to 252.

lines.text: At Nicaea the bishops decree that clergy of those who call themselves Cathari, if they come over, must agree to share communion with the lapsed who have had a period of penance laid on them.
lines.reference: Council of Nicaea, canon 8

lines.text: Nicaea also keeps what it calls the ancient canonical law, that no one at the point of death is to be deprived of the last Viaticum.
lines.reference: Council of Nicaea, canon 13
lines.note: No held source says this rule came from the councils of 251.

lines.text: Socrates says Novatian's church still keeps its strict discipline in Phrygia and Paphlagonia; some found its rule cruel and merciless, others just.
lines.reference: Socrates of Constantinople, Church History IV.28

uncertain: The council's own record is lost. What Carthage decided reaches us through Cyprian, who called it and defended it. What Rome decided reaches us through Eusebius, who summarizes Cornelius's letters.
Novatian's view reaches us through his opponents, and through Socrates of Constantinople almost two centuries later.
The months are Hefele's reconstruction. No held source of the time names them.

Hefele says some older editors and historians turned these two councils into four. He also doubts a council at Antioch on the Novatians that the Libellus Synodicus reports. Eusebius says Dionysius was invited to a synod at Antioch where some were trying to strengthen Novatian's party; Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, thinks it probably met, while Hefele and others doubt it.

Whether the presbyter Novatus of Carthage was one of the five presbyters cut off with Felicissimus is disputed. Hefele says some assert it and others deny it. Leclercq, following Paul Monceaux, says he was.

Whether Cornelius took back those who had sacrificed. Socrates of Constantinople says Novatian broke away because Cornelius received into communion believers who had sacrificed. Cyprian calls the report that Cornelius communicates everywhere with those who sacrificed a false rumor of the apostates, and says Cornelius had only joined with us those whose cause was heard and whose innocence was approved.
The terms for those who had taken certificates. Hefele sums them up as reconciled at once. Cyprian says only that they were admitted in the meantime, after each case was examined.

What Novatian's rule meant. Socrates reports it as leaving the pardon of those who had sacrificed to God. Eusebius, who calls him Novatus, says he acted as if there was no hope of salvation left for them. In McGiffert's English, the Rome decree calls his opinion brother-hating and inhuman.

Whether the quarrel at Carthage began over the lapsed. Hefele, citing Cyprian's letters, says it began over Cyprian's commissioners who carried help to the poor, and over Felicissimus's ordination as deacon by the presbyter Novatus without Cyprian's leave. Only afterward did the party take up the severity of the bishop toward the lapsed as its war-cry.

Cyprian answers a charge. A bishop in Africa, Antonianus, had been shaken by Novatian's letters, and Cyprian writes to clear himself of the thought that he had turned from his early severity to make peace easy for the fallen. He pictures a wounded brother lying stricken on the field of battle, whom Christ urges that he may not wholly perish.

Nicaea's canon 13 keeps what it calls the ancient canonical law, that a man at the point of death must not be deprived of the last Viaticum. Hefele calls the Carthage book the first penitential book of the church. No held source says Nicaea's rules came from these councils.

Alexandria in the same years. Dionysius says the martyrs there received some of the fallen who had sacrificed, once they saw their repentance was enough, and had fellowship with them in prayers and feasts. He had also ordered that the dying who asked for remission should receive it, and tells of the old man Serapion, who had sacrificed and was given a little of the eucharist as he died (Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Church History VI.42 and VI.44).
The year after. The African bishops' letter granting peace to all who kept repenting gives no year. Hefele dates its council to May 252, and the brief tells it as a historian's reckoning.
